screens.title: Why Data Visualization Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Data visualization is the graphical representation of information so humans can perceive patterns, trends, and anomalies faster than by scanning rows and columns. Good visualizations reduce cognitive load: they map numbers to positions, lengths, colors and shapes so you can see a signal quickly. For exploratory analysis, plotting highlights relationships you might miss in summaries — a scatter plot can reveal clusters, while a line chart shows seasonal swings. For communication, a clear plot helps non-technical stakeholders understand your findings without digging into raw data. A concrete example: a table of monthly visitor counts hides a steady upward trend you would immediately see with a simple line plot. A common misconception is that visualization is mere decoration; in fact, a poorly chosen chart can mislead, so selecting the right plot type matters. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Why Visualization
Definition

Data visualization explained

Visualization maps data to visual properties so trends and anomalies appear immediately. It’s both an exploratory tool and a communication channel.

Concrete example
Monthly visitor numbers in a table are hard to scan. A line plot reveals direction and rate of change at a glance.
Misconception
Visualization is decoration. In reality, the wrong chart type can mislead; choose plots to answer questions, not to beautify data.
Why it matters
Decision-makers rely on clear visuals. A single well-labeled chart can drive action faster than a long table.
Analogy

Maps vs spreadsheets

Think of visualization like a map: it shows spatial relationships at a glance. A spreadsheet is like an address list — useful, but not a map.

Check your understanding
  • What question are you trying to answer with your data?
  • Does your intended plot type show that relationship clearly?
  • Are labels present so others can understand the plot without the raw data?
Key Takeaway

Visualization is a core analysis tool that makes patterns obvious; choose the plot that directly answers your question.

screens.title: Matplotlib and pyplot
screens.narratorSegment: Matplotlib is the foundational plotting library in Python, and pyplot is a convenience interface that makes plotting simple and scriptable. Importing matplotlib. pyplot as plt gives you functions that map directly to plotting actions: create a figure, add lines or bars, set titles, and render or save the output. The pyplot interface behaves like a thin state machine: the last plotted figure is the one functions act on unless you explicitly create a new figure. For example, calling the plot function with x and y arrays draws a line, then calling title and xlabel attaches descriptive text to the current axes. A common pitfall is assuming multiple figures are isolated without creating them explicitly — use plt. figure() to start a new canvas when needed. Another subtlety is that plt. show() displays and may clear state in some environments, so it’s best practice to save your figure with plt. savefig() before you call show. Practically, pyplot lets you produce reproducible scripts you can run end to end, which is why we favor it for static plots in analysis pipelines. Try importing pyplot and plotting small arrays to get a feel for the order of operations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Matplotlib & pyplot
What it is

Matplotlib and pyplot

Matplotlib is a comprehensive plotting library. pyplot is the small, MATLAB-like interface you’ll use most for basic static plots.

Common actions
  • Import pyplot as plt
  • Call plt.plot, plt.bar, or plt.scatter
  • Set titles and labels, then save or show
Pitfall
Assuming state isolation between figures. Always call plt.figure() when you need a fresh canvas.
Starter code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Small example: simple line
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)
y = np.sin(x)

plt.figure(figsize=(8,4))
plt.plot(x, y, color='blue', label='sine')
plt.title('Sine wave')
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('sin(x)')
plt.legend()
plt.savefig('sine_wave.png', dpi=150)
plt.show()
This minimal script shows the pyplot workflow: create figure, plot data, label, save, then show. Saving before showing keeps output consistent across environments.

screens.title: Line Plots: Trends over time
screens.narratorSegment: Line plots show how a numeric quantity changes over an ordered domain, typically time. To make a clear line plot, you need x and y arrays of matching length, meaningful axis labels, and an informative title. In practice you often use numeric day indices, timestamps, or a sequence like months on the x-axis and the measured variable on the y-axis. For example, plotting daily temperatures over a week uses a simple call to plot with days as x and temperatures as y, and then you add a grid and labels for readability. A common misuse is to plot categorical data with lines; if the x-axis is not truly ordered, a line will suggest continuity where there is none. Another practical point: adjust figure size for aspect ratio, and use markers when you have few points so individual observations are visible. The example code here shows a complete script that you can run to generate and save a daily temperature trend image. After running, inspect the axes and title to ensure the trend is communicated clearly. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Line Plots
Example
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

# Daily temperatures
days = np.arange(1, 8)
temps = [20, 22, 21, 23, 25, 24, 26]

plt.plot(days, temps, marker='o', color='tab:blue')
plt.title('Daily Temperature Trend')
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Temperature (°C)')
plt.grid(True)
plt.savefig('temperature_trend.png', dpi=300)
plt.show()
This script demonstrates the core steps: data arrays, plot call, labels, grid for readability, and saving with a high resolution.
Guidance
  • Use markers for small data sets so individual points are visible.
  • Ensure x is ordered; avoid lines for categories without order.
  • Adjust figure size with plt.figure(figsize=(w,h)) for display or export needs.
Key Takeaway

Use line plots for continuous or ordered data and label axes; avoid misleading continuity for unordered categories.

screens.title: Bar Charts: Comparing categories
screens.narratorSegment: Bar charts are ideal when you need to compare discrete categories. They map each category to a rectangular bar whose height or length encodes the measured value. Use a bar chart when categories are distinct — for example, sales by product category — and avoid using bars to show relationships between two continuous variables. When labels are long or overlap, rotate the x-axis tick labels and adjust horizontal alignment so readers can read them easily. Setting figure size helps prevent cramped bars and overlapping text. Also choose color intentionally: one color for a single series, or distinct colors when you want to emphasize categories. Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Bar Charts
Code Example
# Sales by product category
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

categories = ['Electronics', 'Clothing', 'Books', 'Home Goods']
sales = [15000, 10000, 7000, 12000]

plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.bar(categories, sales, color=['skyblue','lightcoral','lightgreen','gold'])
plt.title('Total Sales by Product Category')
plt.xlabel('Product Category')
plt.ylabel('Total Sales ($)')
plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('sales_by_category.png')
plt.show()
Practical tips
  • Rotate x-ticks when labels overlap; use ha='right' for alignment.
  • Use plt.figure to control aspect ratio; wider figures help many categories.
  • Color choices should aid interpretation, not distract; use palettes for consistency.
Misuse to avoid
Do not use bar charts to imply a continuous relationship between categories. Bars represent separate groups.
Key Takeaway

Bar charts make categorical comparisons clear; adjust rotation and size to maintain label readability.

screens.title: Scatter Plots: Relationships between two variables
screens.narratorSegment: Scatter plots display pairs of numeric values as points on a two-dimensional plane, which makes them the right choice for assessing relationships or correlations between two variables. Each observation becomes one marker whose x and y coordinates represent the two variables of interest. For example, plotting study hours versus exam scores can reveal whether more study relates to higher scores. When there are many points, use alpha transparency to reduce overplotting and help density patterns emerge. You can also vary marker size to encode a third variable like population or weight. A common mistake is interpreting correlation as causation; scatter plots show association, not proof of cause. Another pitfall is using identical colors and sizes for very dense data without transparency, which hides clusters. The example code uses marker size, color, and alpha to produce a readable scatter plot and adds a dashed grid line for reference. In practical terms, reveal correlation and clusters with markers and transparency. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Scatter Plots
Example
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

study_hours = [2,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12]
exam_scores = [60,65,70,75,80,85,90,92,95,98]

plt.scatter(study_hours, exam_scores, color='purple', marker='o', s=100, alpha=0.7)
plt.title('Study Hours vs. Exam Scores')
plt.xlabel('Study Hours per Week')
plt.ylabel('Exam Score')
plt.grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.6)
plt.savefig('study_vs_score.png')
plt.show()
Interpretation tips
  • Look for trend direction and spread: positive, negative, or none.
  • Use alpha to handle overlap and s to change marker size for importance.
  • Remember: association does not imply causation; be cautious in claims.
Common mistake
Overplotting without transparency can hide clusters; use alpha or binning to reveal density.
Key Takeaway

Scatter plots are the tool of choice for relationships; design markers and transparency to keep dense plots readable.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Customization
Multiple lines & legend
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 100)
y1 = np.sin(x)
y2 = np.cos(x)

plt.plot(x, y1, label='Sine Wave', color='blue', linestyle='-')
plt.plot(x, y2, label='Cosine Wave', color='red', linestyle='--')
plt.title('Sine and Cosine Waves')
plt.xlabel('X-axis')
plt.ylabel('Y-axis')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.savefig('sine_cosine.png')
plt.show()
Style tips
  • Always label axes with units where applicable.
  • Use legends when multiple datasets appear in the same axes; include labels in plot calls.
  • Prefer subtle grid lines and consistent color palettes.
Misleading scaling
Avoid truncating axes to exaggerate differences without noting it; be transparent about axis ranges to maintain trust.
Key Takeaway

Effective styling is functional: it helps readers interpret the plotted data quickly and accurately.

screens.title: Axis Limits, Ticks, and Annotations
screens.narratorSegment: Axes and ticks control how viewers read numerical values. Setting axis limits with plt. xlim and plt. ylim focuses attention on a relevant range, and customizing ticks with plt. xticks and plt. yticks improves legibility. For categorical axes you may supply your own tick positions and labels. Annotations let you highlight a single data point or region using plt. text or plt. annotate, which places text at a coordinate with optional arrows. For example, you might annotate the highest sales month to explain an external campaign. Be careful with axis choices: starting the y-axis above zero on a bar chart can exaggerate differences, which is misleading. A concrete practice: set axis limits only to clarify, not to misrepresent, and add a short annotation when a single point needs context. These small refinements often determine whether a plot tells a trustworthy story or an ambiguous one. screens.title: Common Mistakes in Visualization
screens.narratorSegment: There are a few recurring errors beginners make when creating plots. First, missing labels and titles: without context, a chart becomes ambiguous. Second, choosing the wrong plot type: for example, using a line to connect unordered categories implies continuity that doesn't exist. Third, overlapping elements and small figure size: too many ticks or dense markers make interpretation hard. Fourth, misleading scales: truncating the y-axis on bar charts can exaggerate differences. Finally, forgetting to save figures or saving at too low a resolution results in poor reproductions in reports. To correct these, always add title and axis labels, match the plot type to the data semantics, rotate tick labels when necessary or increase figure size, and check axis ranges for integrity. A quick checklist after plotting helps: read the title, verify axis labels and units, check legend presence, and confirm saved file quality. Adopting these habits prevents miscommunication and preserves the credibility of your analysis. fullNarratorScript:
Visualization is the bridge between raw numbers and insights. In this lesson you will learn why visualizing data matters for both exploration and communication, and how Matplotlib’s pyplot gives you a simple, reproducible way to create publication-quality static plots. We’ll start with the most common plot types — line plots for trends, bar charts for category comparisons, and scatter plots for relationships — and then practice customizing titles, axis labels, legends, colors, and annotations so your charts are clear and honest. You’ll also learn the practical detail of saving figures before you display them, which is crucial when producing figures for reports or presentations. Throughout, expect short, readable code examples you can run immediately and a hands-on activity plotting monthly website traffic. By the end you will be able to pick the right basic plot for a question, style it for clarity, and export it for sharing. Consider how a simple line chart might reveal seasonal trends that a table could hide — that is the practical power we will unlock together.

In this chapter you will build four practical skills that form the foundation of everyday plotting. First, you will learn to choose effective visual forms so you can spot trends, outliers and relationships quickly. Second, you will become comfortable with Matplotlib’s pyplot interface, which is the most direct way in Python to produce static plots you can save and share. Third, you will practice creating the three core plot types — line, bar and scatter — and learn when each is appropriate. Finally, you will learn how to add clear titles, axis labels, legends, and colors so your visualizations communicate without ambiguity. Each objective focuses on a small, testable competency: selecting a plot type, writing working pyplot code, styling axes and labels, and exporting figures at publication resolution. These skills let you move from cleaned arrays or a DataFrame to a figure that someone else can understand within seconds. Consider how each skill reduces misinterpretation and increases the chance your analysis will be acted upon.

This second objectives screen organizes four practice goals you will use during the live coding segments. First, create a line plot that makes a time-based trend obvious, such as daily temperatures or website visitors. Second, build a bar chart that compares categories and handles long labels by rotating ticks. Third, produce a scatter plot that reveals correlations and use marker transparency to reduce overplotting. Fourth, practice saving figures in multiple formats and resolutions so your images are presentation-ready. Each goal has a simple verification step: the plot must include a clear title and axis labels, the axes must be readable, legends should appear where appropriate, and saved files must open correctly at the chosen resolution. These practice goals are intentionally small so you can complete them during short coding sessions and then iterate on style and clarity.

Data visualization is the graphical representation of information so humans can perceive patterns, trends, and anomalies faster than by scanning rows and columns. Good visualizations reduce cognitive load: they map numbers to positions, lengths, colors and shapes so you can see a signal quickly. For exploratory analysis, plotting highlights relationships you might miss in summaries — a scatter plot can reveal clusters, while a line chart shows seasonal swings. For communication, a clear plot helps non-technical stakeholders understand your findings without digging into raw data. A concrete example: a table of monthly visitor counts hides a steady upward trend you would immediately see with a simple line plot. A common misconception is that visualization is mere decoration; in fact, a poorly chosen chart can mislead, so selecting the right plot type matters. To avoid that, ask what question you want the visualization to answer before plotting. Key takeaway: visualization is not optional — it’s an analytic method that converts numbers into insight. How would your next analysis be clearer with a single well-labeled chart? Why Data Visualization Matters means visualization is a method of analysis that reveals patterns and supports communication; choose charts that answer your question.. In practical terms, from tables to patterns: what visualization reveals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Matplotlib is the foundational plotting library in Python, and pyplot is a convenience interface that makes plotting simple and scriptable. Importing matplotlib. pyplot as plt gives you functions that map directly to plotting actions: create a figure, add lines or bars, set titles, and render or save the output. The pyplot interface behaves like a thin state machine: the last plotted figure is the one functions act on unless you explicitly create a new figure. For example, calling the plot function with x and y arrays draws a line, then calling title and xlabel attaches descriptive text to the current axes. A common pitfall is assuming multiple figures are isolated without creating them explicitly — use plt. figure() to start a new canvas when needed. Another subtlety is that plt. show() displays and may clear state in some environments, so it’s best practice to save your figure with plt. savefig() before you call show. Practically, pyplot lets you produce reproducible scripts you can run end to end, which is why we favor it for static plots in analysis pipelines. Try importing pyplot and plotting small arrays to get a feel for the order of operations.

Line plots show how a numeric quantity changes over an ordered domain, typically time. To make a clear line plot, you need x and y arrays of matching length, meaningful axis labels, and an informative title. In practice you often use numeric day indices, timestamps, or a sequence like months on the x-axis and the measured variable on the y-axis. For example, plotting daily temperatures over a week uses a simple call to plot with days as x and temperatures as y, and then you add a grid and labels for readability. A common misuse is to plot categorical data with lines; if the x-axis is not truly ordered, a line will suggest continuity where there is none. Another practical point: adjust figure size for aspect ratio, and use markers when you have few points so individual observations are visible. The example code here shows a complete script that you can run to generate and save a daily temperature trend image. After running, inspect the axes and title to ensure the trend is communicated clearly. Line Plots: Trends over time means line plots reveal trends over an ordered x-axis; avoid using lines when x is categorical without natural order.. In practical terms, create readable line charts for ordered data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Bar charts are ideal when you need to compare discrete categories. They map each category to a rectangular bar whose height or length encodes the measured value. Use a bar chart when categories are distinct — for example, sales by product category — and avoid using bars to show relationships between two continuous variables. When labels are long or overlap, rotate the x-axis tick labels and adjust horizontal alignment so readers can read them easily. Setting figure size helps prevent cramped bars and overlapping text. Also choose color intentionally: one color for a single series, or distinct colors when you want to emphasize categories. The example code provided creates a bar chart with a specified figure size, a custom color list, rotated tick labels for readability, and tight layout to prevent clipping. This combination produces a clean, shareable figure ready for inclusion in a report. Scatter plots display pairs of numeric values as points on a two-dimensional plane, which makes them the right choice for assessing relationships or correlations between two variables. Each observation becomes one marker whose x and y coordinates represent the two variables of interest. When there are many points, use alpha transparency to reduce overplotting and help density patterns emerge. You can also vary marker size to encode a third variable like population or weight. A common mistake is interpreting correlation as causation; scatter plots show association, not proof of cause. Another pitfall is using identical colors and sizes for very dense data without transparency, which hides clusters. There are a few recurring errors beginners make when creating plots. First, missing labels and titles: without context, a chart becomes ambiguous. Second, choosing the wrong plot type: for example, using a line to connect unordered categories implies continuity that doesn't exist. Third, overlapping elements and small figure size: too many ticks or dense markers make interpretation hard. Fourth, misleading scales: truncating the y-axis on bar charts can exaggerate differences. Finally, forgetting to save figures or saving at too low a resolution results in poor reproductions in reports. To correct these, always add title and axis labels, match the plot type to the data semantics, rotate tick labels when necessary or increase figure size, and check axis ranges for integrity.
